title: The orchestration layer
summary: What orchestrators do, how Airflow, Dagster and Prefect model work differently, and how to build idempotent, data-aware pipelines.

blocks.text: 30.1 What an orchestrator actually does

An orchestrator decides *what runs, when, in which order, and what happens when it fails*. It does not move data itself: Spark, Snowflake, dbt or an ingestion tool do. It is the control plane that starts work, watches it and records outcomes.

items: **Scheduling**: time-based triggers (cron, `@daily`) and event-based triggers (a file landed, an upstream table changed).
**Dependencies**: a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of work, so `stg_orders` never runs before `raw_orders` has loaded.
**Retries and timeouts**: transient failures are retried with backoff; hung tasks are killed.
**Backfills**: re-running a past range of intervals, for example every day of March after a logic fix.
**SLAs and alerting**: the finance mart must be ready by 06:00, or someone is paged.
**Run history**: who ran what, with which parameters, and the outcome.

blocks.text: Without one, teams chain cron jobs with sleeps. That works for five jobs and collapses at fifty: the dependency graph is unknown, failures are silent, backfills mean editing scripts.
Keep the orchestrator thin. Business logic belongs in dbt models, Spark jobs or tested Python packages; the orchestrator *calls* them with the right parameters (usually a partition or time window).
30.2 Three mental models: tasks, assets, flows
The tools differ less in features than in what they treat as the primary object.

head: Model
Primary object
Typical tool
Strength
Weakness
rows: Graph describes *steps*, not data; lineage implicit
A data asset (table, file, model) and how it is computed
A Python function (flow) calling other functions (tasks)
Low ceremony, dynamic Python control flow
Little opinion on lineage; structure is up to the team

blocks.text: Airflow is moving towards the asset view: 2.4 added *Datasets* for data-aware scheduling, Airflow 3 renamed them *Assets* and moved authoring imports under `airflow.sdk` (check the current documentation for your version). The category is converging on knowing about data, not only tasks.
30.3 Code: the same pipeline in three tools

blocks.title: Airflow (TaskFlow API)
Dagster (software-defined assets)

blocks.text: In Prefect the same pipeline is a function decorated with `@flow` calling functions decorated with `@task(retries=3)`, parameterised by `day`. The unit differs per tool: an Airflow DAG run for a logical date, a Dagster materialisation of an asset partition, a Prefect flow run with parameters. All three can express this pipeline; the question is which model your team will keep consistent at 400 pipelines.
30.4 Idempotent, partitioned runs and backfills
The key property is **idempotency**: running a job twice for an interval leaves the same state as running it once. Retries and backfills depend on it.

items: **Parameterise by interval, not `now()`**: a job for `2025-03-14` handles that day whenever it runs.
**Overwrite the slice you own**: `INSERT OVERWRITE` a partition, `DELETE` + `INSERT` in one transaction, or a `MERGE` on a natural key. Never blind `INSERT` on retry.
**Guard side effects** (emails, API calls, exports) with a run key.

blocks.title: Owning a partition

blocks.text: A backfill is then many partition runs. Limit concurrency (365 parallel queries will saturate a warehouse), run oldest-first when partitions depend on earlier state (SCD2, cumulative tables), and isolate backfill capacity from the daily schedule.

Airflow's `catchup=True` on a DAG with an old `start_date` silently schedules every missed interval when the DAG is unpaused. Teams have started thousands of runs by accident. Default to `catchup=False` and run backfills deliberately.
30.5 Event-driven and data-aware scheduling
Cron answers *when*, not *is the input ready?*. Running at 02:00 because ingestion usually ends by 01:30 fails the day it takes two hours. Better triggers:

items: **Sensors**: poll for a condition (file or partition exists, upstream succeeded). Long-running sensors occupy worker slots; prefer deferrable or reschedule modes.
**Events**: an object-store notification or a Kafka message triggers a run. Lower latency, no polling.

**Data-aware scheduling**: a run is triggered because an upstream *asset* was updated (Airflow Assets/Datasets, Dagster declarative automation and freshness policies). The scheduler reasons over data, not clocks.

blocks.text: Data-aware triggers also make SLAs meaningful: *`fct_orders` for yesterday was materialised at 05:40, inside its 06:00 objective* (see chapter 33).
30.6 Orchestrating dbt and SQLMesh
Transformation frameworks (chapter 31) have their own internal DAG. Two integration styles exist:

head: Style
How
Pros
Cons
rows: Simple; the framework handles its own order
One failure fails the whole task; no per-model retries or lineage in the orchestrator
The orchestrator parses dbt's `manifest.json` and creates one node per model (e.g. the `dagster-dbt` integration, or Cosmos for Airflow)
Per-model retries, lineage, partial reruns, asset-level freshness
More nodes to schedule; must keep parsing in sync with the project

blocks.text: SQLMesh tracks which intervals of each model are processed; `sqlmesh run` executes only due intervals, so the orchestrator calls it on a cadence without passing dates.

blocks.title: A retail team moves from cron to assets
blocks.text: A retail analytics team ran 60 cron jobs on a VM; finance closes failed when a late ingestion left downstream jobs reading half-loaded data. They moved to an asset-centric orchestrator.
items: Each bronze table became a partitioned asset; dbt models were loaded from the manifest as downstream assets.
Downstream models run when upstreams materialise, with a 06:00 freshness objective for finance marts.
Backfills after logic changes became a selection of partitions in the UI, run with a concurrency limit of 8.

blocks.text: 30.7 Failure modes and operating the orchestrator

items: **Scheduler as single point of failure**: run it highly available or managed, with a heartbeat alert.
**Top-level code in DAG files**: Airflow parses DAG files continuously; a slow import or query at module level degrades the scheduler.
**Passing data through the orchestrator**: XCom and similar mechanisms are for small metadata (paths, row counts), not data frames.
**Alert fatigue**: alert on SLA breaches and repeated failures, not every retried task.

blocks.text: Retries hide flaky upstreams. Track retry counts; a task that succeeds on its third attempt nightly is an incident waiting to happen.

blocks.title: Design the schedule for a three-source revenue mart
blocks.text: You load orders (CDC, continuous), payments (hourly API extract) and FX rates (daily file at about 23:00 UTC). A gold `fct_revenue_daily` must be ready by 07:00 for Europe. Choose the orchestration model, triggers, partitioning and idempotency mechanism for each step, and describe how you would backfill the last 90 days after a currency-conversion bug.
hints: What if the FX file is late or never arrives?
Which steps can run in parallel during the backfill?

items: An orchestrator is a control plane: scheduling, dependencies, retries, backfills, SLAs, run history.
Airflow is task-centric, Dagster asset-centric, Prefect flow-centric; the industry is converging on data-aware scheduling.
Jobs must be idempotent per interval: parameterise by partition, overwrite the owned slice.
Prefer data-aware or event triggers over guessing with cron; express SLAs on assets, not DAG end times.
Integrate dbt either as a black box or as an exploded graph from `manifest.json`; SQLMesh tracks intervals itself.

blocks.q: A daily job appends rows with a plain INSERT. It fails half-way and the orchestrator retries it. What is the core problem?
options: The retry interval is too short
The orchestrator should have used a sensor
The job is not idempotent, so the retry can duplicate rows
blocks.explain: A blind append duplicates data on retry; overwriting the partition or merging on a key makes it idempotent. Changing retries or triggers does not change what the write does.

blocks.q: What distinguishes an asset-centric orchestrator such as Dagster from a task-centric one?
options: Its graph is made of data assets, so lineage and freshness are first-class
It has no scheduler and relies on cron
blocks.explain: Software-defined assets describe the tables or files produced and their dependencies, which makes questions like *is this table fresh?* native. Task-centric tools describe steps; they can still run Python and have schedulers.

blocks.q: A team enables a DAG with start_date one year ago and catchup=True. What happens?
options: Airflow asks for confirmation before backfilling
The scheduler creates runs for every missed interval since start_date
blocks.explain: Catchup fills every missed interval, possibly hundreds of runs, without confirmation. Hence `catchup=False` plus deliberate backfills.

blocks.q: Why do teams prefer data-aware triggers over a fixed 02:00 cron for downstream models?
options: Cron cannot run more than once a day
Data-aware triggers run only when inputs have actually been updated, avoiding reads of incomplete data
Data-aware triggers are always cheaper in compute
blocks.explain: The risk with cron is running before the upstream is complete; asset triggers wait for the data. Cron supports any frequency and retries, and cost is not inherently lower.
